This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
House Republicans have beaten back an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The House, for Tuesday, voted 211 to 204 to effectively block impeachment charges from being considered.
Earlier in the day, Hegseth held his first press conference at the Pentagon in six months.
It appears David folk and flick.
I'd say he was tense and intense.
And what was clear is throughout his remarks, he wrapped himself in President Trump and in the troops as though he was their shield and their protector.
Here's a sound bite of what I mean.
Put the secretary on trial today and the men and women who carried out those orders tomorrow.
If they want to come for the warriors, they're going to have to come through me.
That seemed like an inversion of what was happening.
He wanted to use them to shield him.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffery says Democrats will have a conversation about impeaching Hegseth when they take control of Congress in January.
U.S. boycotting a key U.N. human rights review for the second year running, the only country ever to do so.
The process, the last resort for victims of alleged violations to testify before the U.N.
The Trump administration says the process is biased, as imaging folks reports.
U.S. human rights groups led by the American Civil Liberties Union traveled to Geneva with evidence of alleged ill-treatment of migrants and protesters.
U.N. diplomats wanted to ask their U.S. counterparts about the use of the death penalty, restrictions on abortion and lethal attacks on boats in the Caribbean, viewed by many as illegal.
But Washington was a no-show. The U.S. has already left the U.N. Human Rights Council and says it has no interest in being lectured.
But the review process is not supposed to be optional, and the U.N. now has to decide how to react.
For NPR News, I'm Imogen Folks in Geneva.
Asian shares largely advancing after Wall Street slumped following the Labor Department's higher-than-expected report on inflation.
Investors think the Federal Reserve will respond by raising interest rates next month. Here's NPR's Scott Horsley.
The government's latest cost-of-living index shows consumer prices rose by four-tenths of one percent in October.
Rising rents accounted for about a third of that increase. Grocery costs were also up sharply.
The monthly inflation rate was higher than forecasters had expected and shows prices continue to climb faster than average wages.
The Federal Reserve was already expected to try to curb inflation by raising its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point next month.
Fed Governor Chris Waller says a larger half-point rate hike could be warranted.
The prospect of higher short-term borrowing costs rippled through the bond market yields on 10-year treasuries rose, which tends to put upward pressure on mortgage rates.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
And you're listening to NPR News.
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer says he is confident he will be elected Senate Majority Leader when Democrats take control of Congress in January.
But he is facing opposition independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Michigan Senator Alyssa Slotkin have come out against his candidacy, with Sanders saying Tuesday that he respects Schumer but that the time is now for change.
A handful of incoming Senate Democrats have also declined to support Schumer.
On the GOP side, Senate Republicans Tuesday opted to keep John Thune of South Dakota as their leader.
House Republicans chose Judiciary Chairman and Trump ally Jim Jordan of Ohio.
Washington State produces millions of pounds of pumpkins every year.
Northwest Public Broadcasting's Lauren Gallup visited some farms to find out what happens to all those pumpkins that don't get picked after Halloween.
When Double R Farms closes its pumpkin patch for the year, the leftovers don't go to waste.
Instead, the fowl and fauna.
They have a feast right now.
As Jerry Ruiz walks down a gravel path from her house to the fields, flocks fly overhead and land in the fields of mowed down pumpkins and the old corn maze.
All the geese are loving it right now, and they've already been over to the pumpkins and the crows also. Crows and the Canadian geese.
Ruiz says after a few weeks, the birds are done with the crop.
The rest decomposes and goes back into the soil, adding nutrients for next year's harvest.
For NPR News, I'm Lauren Gallup in Puyallup, Washington.
And I'm Giles Snyder. This is NPR News.

topics.text: House Republicans block effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, vote 211 to 204
U.S. boycotts UN human rights review for second year, with rights groups testifying in Geneva
Consumer prices rise 0.4% in October, higher than expected, boosting Fed rate hike odds
Chuck Schumer says he is confident of becoming Senate Majority Leader despite opposition
Senate Republicans keep John Thune as leader; House Republicans choose Jim Jordan
Washington pumpkin farms let geese, crows, and decomposition consume unsold pumpkins after Halloween
